article.headline: Solo Developer Outpaces Google on Its Own KV Cache Algorithm
article.lede: When Google published a research paper on compressing the memory used by large language models during inference, it released no working code. Tom Turney, a solo developer, read the paper, rebuilt the algorithm from scratch using Claude in seven days, then optimised it until it ran 3.7 times faster than the baseline — and got a 35-billion-parameter model running on a MacBook.
article.body:
The core problem Turney tackled is the *KV cache* — the memory a transformer model accumulates as it processes text. During inference, every token the model has seen must be stored as key-value pairs so attention heads can refer back to them. For long conversations or large models, this cache grows enormous: a 35B-parameter model can exhaust consumer GPU memory long before it exhausts its context window. Quantisation — reducing each stored number from 16 or 32 bits to just 2 or 3 — shrinks that footprint dramatically, at the cost of some precision.

Turney's implementation, **TurboQuant+**, composes two algorithms. The first, *PolarQuant*, applies a random rotation to the cache vectors and then performs scalar quantisation on each coordinate independently; because the rotation redistributes values into a near-uniform *Beta distribution*, a small fixed set of centroids can represent them efficiently with b−1 bits. The second, *QJL* (Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss), handles the residual error left after PolarQuant using a single sign bit per dimension, exploiting the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma's guarantee that random projections approximately preserve distances. Together they achieve roughly b bits per coordinate — comparable to what Google's paper described.

The engineering leap was moving from a Python prototype to hand-tuned C and GPU kernels. According to the LinkedIn summary drawn from the project, throughput climbed from 739 tokens per second to 2,747 tokens per second, a 3.7× gain. Turney also added ideas not in the Google paper: *sparse value compression* (skipping near-zero values in the cache entirely) and *temporal decay* (weighting older cache entries as less important). The 4.6× cache compression ratio cited in the tweet is what makes a 35B model tractable on a MacBook with unified memory, which has bandwidth advantages over discrete GPU setups.

The broader point the bookmark is making — and it is worth taking seriously — is about the changing shape of research replication. A paper that would once have required a team of ML engineers with access to a cluster was reconstructed, optimised, and extended by one developer in a week. The AI pair-programming assist from Claude handled much of the scaffolding and boilerplate, letting Turney focus on the algorithmic substance. That asymmetry, between a research organisation that can publish but not ship, and a solo developer who can ship before the organisation does, is new.

concepts.definition: Short for key-value cache. In transformer language models, every layer computes 'keys' and 'values' from each input token; these are stored so later tokens can attend to earlier ones without recomputation. The cache grows linearly with context length and can become the dominant memory cost for long conversations or large models.

The practice of storing cached key-value tensors in fewer bits than the original 16- or 32-bit floats. Going from 16 bits to 2 bits per value can shrink the cache eightfold, at the cost of introducing small numerical errors. The research challenge is choosing a quantisation scheme whose errors degrade model quality as little as possible.

A classical result in mathematics showing that any set of points in high-dimensional space can be projected down to a lower-dimensional space using a random linear map, with pairwise distances approximately preserved. In QJL, only the sign of each projected coordinate is kept (one bit), which is enough to reconstruct approximate inner products — the operation at the heart of attention.

A quantisation method that first applies a random rotation matrix to a vector (spreading its variance evenly across dimensions), then applies scalar quantisation coordinate-by-coordinate. Because the rotated coordinates follow a near-uniform Beta distribution, a small fixed codebook of centroids works well for all of them, making the scheme efficient to implement.

Compressing a floating-point number by mapping it to the nearest value in a small discrete set (a 'codebook'). Two-bit scalar quantisation uses four possible values; the challenge is choosing those four values to minimise average error for the distribution of numbers being compressed.

repos.summary: TurboQuant+ is an open-source Python and C/CUDA implementation of a KV cache quantisation algorithm derived from a Google research paper. It composes PolarQuant and QJL to achieve roughly b bits per coordinate of cache storage, with additional techniques — sparse value compression and temporal decay — not present in the original paper. Benchmarks show 3.7× throughput improvement over the Python baseline and sufficient compression to run a 35B-parameter model on Apple Silicon.

ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.

The account covers breaking crypto news, market analysis, memecoin trends, DeFi, and geopolitical events, often drawing hundreds of thousands of live listeners. With over 155,000 followers, it is one of the most prominent crypto discussion platforms on X.
